title: The month of Sawan
hook: in Sawan the bride blossoms who loves His lotus feet (Barah Maha, ang 134)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asarh, and your line: asarh: keep him near. Who did you cool down? After all that waiting, the clouds finally break. Day five hundred seventy.

Anyone who has lived through a North Indian summer remembers the first real rain. The smell hits before the drops do: wet dust, sharp and sweet. Then the sky opens. Kids run out into the street. Peacocks call from the fields. Within days, cracked brown ground turns green, and in Punjabi villages, swings go up in the trees, and girls and women gather to sing the songs of Teeyan. Sawan, July into August, is the month the whole land seems to exhale. And in the folk barah maha, it's the month the waiting bride feels most alive, and most alone.
screen: `THE SMELL OF THE FIRST RAIN.` → `BROWN GROUND TURNS GREEN.` → `SWINGS IN THE TREES.`

segments.voice: The Sawan stanza is on ang 134. In paraphrase: in Sawan, the bride blossoms who loves the lotus feet of the Lord. Sarsee, she blossoms, she flourishes, the way the land does when the rain comes. Her mind and body are dyed in true love; the Name alone is her support. Then a contrast. The pleasures of poison, as the stanza calls them, are false; everything that's seen of them turns to ash. And then the rain image, turned inside out. The drop of the Lord's nectar is beautiful, the stanza says, and those who meet the holy ones drink it in. The forests and the meadows are refreshed by the One, the all-powerful, the infinite. Look at what Guru Arjan does with the monsoon. In the folk songs, the rain is what makes the separated woman ache: everyone else is together under the swings. In this stanza, the rain is what happens to the soul that loves the One. She's the land. The love is the rain. And she doesn't just survive the season; she blossoms. Sawan is the first month in this Barah Maha that sounds almost like arrival. It isn't all joy; the warning about false pleasures turning to ash is still there. But the main image is green. After two months of heat, Jeth and Asarh, where the lesson was bowing and keeping the One near, Sawan shows what that kind of nearness looks like when it rains. The lotus feet, charan kamal, is an old and tender image in Indian devotion, and Gurbani uses it often: the Beloved's feet, soft as a lotus, are where the devotee comes to rest.
screen: `SARSEE: SHE BLOSSOMS.` · `FALSE PLEASURES TURN TO ASH.` · `A DROP OF THE LORD'S NECTAR.` · `THE SOUL IS THE LAND; LOVE IS THE RAIN.` · then, large: `SAWAN: BLOSSOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch rain or water. If it's raining where you are, watch it at a window. If not, run a tap slowly, or pour a glass of water and watch it fill, or simply picture rain on dry ground. Notice the first drops darkening the dust. Breathe slowly and let the picture soften something in you that's been dry. Let it be watered without needing to understand it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Sawan. The monsoon month: the bride who loves the Lord's lotus feet blossoms, like land under the rain, and drinks the drop of nectar.
Your line: sawan: blossom. Today, water one thing: a plant, a friendship, a neglected part of your own day. Day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: On the sangrand of Sawan, many gurdwaras read the Sawan stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, while in Punjab the monsoon month is also marked by the folk festival of Teeyan.

what it means: the soul that loves the One is like land under the monsoon: it blossoms.
what a scholar hears: 'saavan sarsee kaamnee charan kamal siu piaar'; Guru Arjan turns the folk barah maha's month of loneliness into a month of blossoming.
